newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian economy under threat from currency slide.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian economy under threat from currency slide.

text.p: Economic stability, touted by Nigeria's military government as one of its main successes in the last two years, no longer seems a sure bet among economists.
They argue that a nearly 10 percent depreciation in the value of the naira currency since January could destabilise one of sub-Saharan Africa's biggest economy.
"If the rate at which the naira is falling continues unchecked then we will be back to the situation before the reforms of 1995," says banker Odima Okoronkwo.
This means manufacturers and other investors will return to uncertainty and not be able to plan ahead about how much it will cost them to run their businesses in import-dependent Nigeria.
But the authorities dismiss the panic as "unpatriotic."

Finance minister Anthony Ani and central bank governor Paul Ogwuma said in a joint statement in the capital Abuja on Tuesday that there were no plans to further devalue the naira after its 5.88 percent devaluation to 85 naira to $1 six weeks ago.

"With the current external reserve position of over $6 billion compared with $1.5 billion in the same period of 1996, the government is in a better position to defend the naira at all cost," they added.

In 1995, General Sani Abacha launched cautious reforms, legalising the autonomous foreign exchange market (AFEM) and slashing public spending which by last year had stabilised the rate of the naira at around 80 to the dollar and reduced inflation to less than 30 percent from about 80 percent.
Despite its recent devaluation the naira remains under pressure, selling at 90 to $1 in several places in the country.
This has worrying implications for inflation rising again.

The latest Federal Office of Statistics report puts inflation in February at 24.4 percent, down from 26.7 percent in the preceding month but says that food prices actually rose a little while prices of manufactured items fell.
Harder-hit is the weekly foreign exchange auction where the demand for dollars has risen sharply to around $100 million compared to the weekly demand of about $60 million last year.
Commentators say at current demand government's provision of $2.7 billion for the AFEM will be exhausted before August, spelling doom for a key facet of Nigeria's economic policy.

"The economic successes of the regime are being daily eroded, interestingly by factors which analysts say the administration itself contrived," wrote the independent Thisday newspaper in an editorial on Friday.

"Before this development, the fine points of the General Sani Abacha regime have been relatively stable exchange rate, plummeting inflation and a general positive stability in order macro-economic aggregates," it added.
The recent problems stem from a reflationary budget announced in January to spur economic growth.

Given lack of foreign investments because of political instability, the government opted instead to increase domestic spending with an avowed aim to achieve gross domestic product growth of 5.5 percent compared to 3.3 percent last year.

The business community and particularly the oil industry, Nigeria's economic engine were disappointed because what they had been led to believe was that there would be privatisation of loss-making and in-efficient state enterprises in 1997.
When the budget was unveiled, Abacha only promised to set up a committee to study the issue of privatisation and five months into the year the committee is yet to be appointed.
"Without privatisation no new money will come into Nigeria," says a western diplomat who watches the economy, adding "The risk of political instability is also too great."
The instability was precipitated in 1993 when the army annulled a presidential election to restore democracy.
Scores of people including business tycoon Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the annulled vote, are detained without trial, making Nigeria a pariah state to the West.

The West, like the Nigerian opposition is suspicious of Abacha's transition to civil rule, which he says will lead to a handover to a democratically-elected president next year but which many people think is a ruse to perpetuate his rule.

"(Nigeria) needs to do more in the political arena, through a more transparent implementation of the transition programme and the release of detainees to make it reconcile with the demands of the international community , whose cooperation it badly needs to succeed in the economic front," wrote Thisday.

Economists also say to attract foreign investment, Nigeria must merge the official exchange rate of 22 naira to the dollar, which ensures the military government gets foreign exchange at a preferential rate with the AFEM rate for uniformity.
"We are agreed that merging is necessary but it is not the solution now...we are carrying out some studies whose outcome will determine a lot of things," says finance minister Ani.
Officials say Nigeria's ultimate aim is to build an external reserve base of $12 billion by October 1998 and then make the naira convertible.
